title: Property Investment for Beginners: 8 Questions to Answer Before You Buy
description: A beginner's checklist for property investment in India, covering goals, true costs, financing, legal checks, tax and exit, with sources and no return promises.
text: Property is a large, slow-moving and expensive purchase. Mistakes are hard to undo. Instead of a list of “tips”, here are eight questions to answer honestly before you commit. 1. What is the property for? Rental income and long-term holding need different properties: For income, what matters is realistic rent, tenant demand and low running costs. For long-term holding, location fundamentals and your ability to keep holding through vacancies or a weak market matter more. Be wary of anyone who promises both, or names a specific future price. 2. What will it really cost to buy? Add the price, stamp duty and registration (in Gujarat, check the official calculator on GARVI), GST if the property is under construction, legal fees, loan fees, society charges and any brokerage. Our first-home guide lists these. 3. What will it cost to hold? Every year: property tax, maintenance or society charges, repairs, insurance, and months without a tenant. Then estimate the net yield: (annual rent − vacancy − annual costs) ÷ total purchase cost × 100 Our residential vs commercial guide has a worked example. 4. Can your finances survive a bad year? If you borrow: Could you pay the EMI for six months with no rent? Could you still pay if the rate rose by one or two percentage points? RBI raised the policy repo rate to 5.50% on 7 October 2026 (RBI), and floating loan rates typically follow. RBI’s lending limits mean a lender usually finances at most 75–90% of the property’s value, depending on the loan size (RBI Master Circular – Housing Finance). 5. Is the title clean and the project registered? Check the land record, title chain, encumbrances, NA order and BU permission. For new projects, check registration on the state RERA portal (GujRERA in Gujarat). Have an advocate do a title search. See the document checklist. 6. How will the income and profit be taxed? Rent is taxed under “income from house property”. A standard deduction of 30% of the annual value is allowed, plus interest on borrowed capital. This is section 22 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly section 24 of the 1961 Act (Income Tax Department). How much of a loss you can set off depends on the tax regime you choose. Profit on sale: property held for more than 24 months is a long-term capital asset. For transfers on or after 23 July 2024, long-term gains are taxed at 12.5% without indexation. Resident individuals and HUFs who acquired the property before that date can compare this with 20% with indexation and pay the lower amount (Income Tax Department). Tax rules are detailed and change with each Budget. Consult a chartered accountant for your own situation. 7. How would you get out? Property can take months to sell, and selling costs money: brokerage, and for the buyer, stamp duty, which affects the price they will pay. Ask how many similar units are for sale nearby and how long they have been listed. A market with a lot of unsold stock is slower to sell into. 8. Is too much of your wealth in one asset? For many households one property is most of their net worth. Ask whether you’d still be comfortable if that property’s value stayed flat for years, or if it sat empty for a while. A short checklist Goal defined: income or long-term holding Full purchase cost calculated Net yield estimated with vacancy and costs EMI stress-tested for a rate rise and six months without rent Title search by an advocate; RERA registration checked Tax position discussed with a chartered accountant Exit plan and realistic time to sell considered Sources GARVI, Inspector General of Registration, Gujarat — https://garvi.gujarat.gov.in/ RBI monetary policy press release, 7 Oct 2026 — https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=63742 RBI Master Circular – Housing Finance, 1 Apr 2025 — https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasCirculardetails.aspx?id=12282 Gujarat Real Estate Regulatory Authority — https://gujrera.gujarat.gov.in/ Income Tax Department: section 22 (Income-tax Act, 2025) — https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-22-211 Income Tax Department: tax on long-term capital gains — https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/tax-on-long-term-capital-gains%E2%80%8B

title: Residential vs Commercial Property: How the Risks and Costs Differ
description: A framework for comparing residential and commercial property, covering income, vacancy, financing, management and liquidity, without unsupported return claims.
text: You’ll often read that commercial property “gives higher rental yields” and residential is “safer”. Both claims are too general to act on. Yields vary widely by city, location, building and tenant, and published averages rarely match the property in front of you. This guide sets out the differences that matter and how to compare two actual properties. How the two differ Factor Residential (flats, houses) Commercial (shops, offices, warehouses) Typical tenant Households Businesses Typical lease Often 11-month agreements, renewed Often longer leases with rent escalation clauses (varies) Vacancy risk Usually a larger pool of potential tenants Fewer suitable tenants; a vacancy can last longer Sensitivity to the economy Housing demand is relatively steady Tied to business conditions in the area Financing Home loans; RBI loan-to-value caps for housing Commercial property loans; terms usually stricter Ticket size Lower entry points available Often higher Fit-out and repairs Owner usually maintains the unit Depends on the lease; tenants sometimes do fit-outs Ease of selling Broad buyer pool Narrower buyer pool Tax on rent Taxed as “income from house property” for both Same head; GST may apply to commercial rent above thresholds (take advice) These are general tendencies, not rules. A well-located shop can be easier to let than a flat in an oversupplied area. Compare net income, not headline yield For any property you’re considering, estimate: Annual rent you can realistically get. Check current listings for comparable units and ask local agents. Minus vacancy: months without a tenant. Assume some, not zero. Minus ongoing costs: property tax, society or maintenance charges, repairs, insurance, letting fees. Total purchase cost: price plus stamp duty, registration, legal fees and any GST or fit-out. Net yield = (annual rent − vacancy loss − annual costs) ÷ total purchase cost × 100 Worked example (illustrative only) Item Assumption Purchase price ₹50,00,000 Stamp duty, registration and legal fees (assumed) ₹3,20,000 Total cost ₹53,20,000 Monthly rent ₹15,000 → ₹1,80,000 a year Vacancy: 1 month a year −₹15,000 Property tax, maintenance and repairs (assumed) −₹30,000 Net annual income ₹1,35,000 Net yield 1,35,000 ÷ 53,20,000 = 2.54% Gross yield on the price alone would be 1,80,000 ÷ 50,00,000 = 3.6%. The difference shows why headline figures flatter. Change any assumption and the result moves. Run the numbers for both properties you’re comparing, with the same care. The example ignores loan interest, income tax and any change in the property’s value. Each can change the outcome substantially. Risks that apply to both Liquidity: property can take months to sell, and transaction costs are high. Concentration: one property is a large share of most people’s wealth. Leverage: a loan magnifies both gains and losses, and EMIs continue during vacancies. Rates can rise; RBI raised the repo rate to 5.50% on 7 October 2026 (RBI). Legal and title risk: see our document checklist. Regulatory protection: registered real estate projects, residential or commercial, are covered by the RERA Act, 2016. Check registration on your state’s RERA portal (in Gujarat, GujRERA). How to decide Ask yourself: Can I afford a long vacancy without missing EMIs? Do I understand who would rent this unit and why? Have I compared net, not gross, income? Could I sell within a reasonable time if I had to? Have I had the title checked by an advocate, and the tax position by a chartered accountant? If you can’t answer these confidently for a commercial property, the lower complexity of residential property may suit you better. That isn’t because residential “returns more”; it’s because its risks are easier to understand and manage. Also read: Questions to answer before your first property investment. Sources RBI monetary policy press release, 7 Oct 2026 — https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=63742 Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 — https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2158/1/a2016-16.pdf Gujarat Real Estate Regulatory Authority — https://gujrera.gujarat.gov.in/ Calculation: the worked example uses the assumptions shown in the table and was recomputed independently.

title: How to Buy Your First Home in Gujarat: A Step-by-Step Guide
description: The order of steps for a first home purchase in Gujarat, covering budget, loan limits, legal checks, stamp duty, TDS and registration, with official sources.
text: This guide walks through a first home purchase in Gujarat in the order things usually happen. Each step links to the official source, so you can confirm current rules. On this page Step 1: Work out the full budget, not just the price Step 2: Check how much you can borrow Step 3: Shortlist and verify the property Step 4: Pay a limited advance and get a written agreement Step 5: Arrange the loan Step 6: Deduct TDS if the price is ₹50 lakh or more Step 7: Pay stamp duty and register the sale deed Step 8: After registration Common first-time mistakes Sources Step 1: Work out the full budget, not just the price The amount you need is the price plus the costs of buying: Stamp duty and registration fee. In Gujarat these are paid on the higher of the agreement value and the government’s jantri (ready reckoner) value. Widely published rates are 4.9% stamp duty and 1% registration fee, with the registration fee waived for women who buy as sole owners. We could not locate the government notification for the women’s concession. Confirm the current figures with the official calculator on GARVI before you budget. GST on under-construction property (not on ready, completed property). Ask the builder for the exact amount in writing. Other costs: legal fees for the title search, loan processing fees, society transfer charges or deposits, maintenance deposits, and brokerage if an agent is involved. Step 2: Check how much you can borrow RBI caps how much of a home’s value a lender can finance (the loan-to-value, or LTV, ratio): Loan amount Maximum LTV Up to ₹30 lakh 90% Above ₹30 lakh, up to ₹75 lakh 80% Above ₹75 lakh 75% The rest is your down payment. For homes above ₹10 lakh, stamp duty and registration are not included in the property cost used for this calculation, so you normally pay them from your own funds. Source: RBI Master Circular – Housing Finance (1 April 2025). Rates are rising. RBI raised the policy repo rate by 0.25 percentage points to 5.50% on 7 October 2026 (RBI press release). Floating home-loan rates linked to the repo rate usually follow. When comparing offers, look at the spread over the benchmark, the processing fee, and how resets work. Prepayment: under RBI’s Pre-payment Charges Directions, 2025, lenders may not charge a prepayment penalty on floating-rate loans to individuals for non-business purposes. This applies to loans sanctioned or renewed from 1 January 2026 (RBI notification). Step 3: Shortlist and verify the property Before paying any token amount: New project: search for it on the GujRERA portal. Check that the registration number, promoter and project details match the advertising, and read the latest quarterly progress update. Any property: check the land record (7/12 and 8A, or the property card), the chain of title, an encumbrance search, the NA order and BU permission. See our document checklist. Visit more than once, at different times of day. Check water supply, drainage, access roads and parking. Step 4: Pay a limited advance and get a written agreement For projects covered by RERA, a promoter may not take more than 10% of the cost as an advance before a written agreement for sale is registered (section 13 of the RERA Act, 2016). The agreement should state: the price the payment schedule the carpet area (the RERA definition) the possession date what happens if possession is delayed Step 5: Arrange the loan Apply with the bank you chose. The lender will do its own legal and technical checks and ask for documents such as the title papers, NA order, approved plan and BU permission. Read the sanction letter for the rate type, the spread, fees, and how EMI or tenure changes when rates reset. Step 6: Deduct TDS if the price is ₹50 lakh or more If the consideration or the stamp duty value is ₹50 lakh or more, the buyer must deduct 1% tax at source from the payment to the seller and deposit it with the government. From 1 April 2026 this falls under section 393 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly section 194-IA of the 1961 Act). It is filed using Form 141, which replaced Form 26QB. See the Income Tax Department’s guidance on section 393 and Form 141. Different rules apply if the seller is a non-resident; take professional advice. Step 7: Pay stamp duty and register the sale deed Buy e-stamp paper or pay stamp duty through the channels listed on GARVI. Book a sub-registrar appointment. Buyer, seller and two witnesses attend with original ID to execute and register the sale deed. Keep the registered deed and its index copy safely. Step 8: After registration Apply to update the land record (mutation) or property card, and the property tax record, in your name. Transfer the society membership, and the electricity, water and gas connections. Keep every receipt. You’ll need them for tax purposes and if you sell later. Common first-time mistakes Budgeting only for the price and the down payment, and forgetting stamp duty, registration and GST. Paying a token before checking documents and RERA registration. Relying on the bank’s approval as proof of clean title. Forgetting to deduct and deposit TDS on purchases of ₹50 lakh or more. Sources GARVI, Inspector General of Registration, Gujarat — https://garvi.gujarat.gov.in/ — accessed 23 Oct 2026. RBI Master Circular – Housing Finance, 1 Apr 2025 — https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewMasCirculardetails.aspx?id=12282 RBI monetary policy press release, 7 Oct 2026 — https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/BS_PressReleaseDisplay.aspx?prid=63742 RBI (Pre-payment Charges on Loans) Directions, 2025 — https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/NotificationUser.aspx?Id=12878&Mode=0 Gujarat Real Estate Regulatory Authority — https://gujrera.gujarat.gov.in/ Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 — https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2158/1/a2016-16.pdf Income Tax Department, section 393 and Form 141 — https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/section-393-5 ; https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/help/all-topics/e-filing-services/form-141-challan-cum-statement-deduction-tax-us-3931 Secondary sources for Gujarat stamp duty rates (pending official confirmation): ClearTax, HomeFirst.

title: Documents to Check Before Buying Property in Gujarat: A Practical Checklist
description: What each key property document proves, where to get it in Gujarat (AnyROR, GARVI, GujRERA), and the warning signs to look for before you pay.
text: Buying property in Gujarat means checking two things: who owns it and whether it can legally be used the way you intend. The documents below answer those questions. For each one, this guide explains what it proves, where to find it, and what should make you stop and ask questions. On this page The checklist at a glance Land records: 7/12, 8A and mutation entries Property card for city survey areas Title deeds and the chain of ownership Encumbrance search on GARVI NA order: can the land be used for a home? Approved plan and BU permission GujRERA registration for new projects Dues, society NOC and the seller’s identity Common mistakes What to do next Sources The checklist at a glance Document What it tells you Where to check 7/12 extract (VF-7) and 8A (VF-8A) Who holds the land, its area, tenure and recorded rights, for rural and agricultural survey numbers AnyROR (view) / iORA (certified copies, applications) Mutation entries (VF-6) How ownership changed over time (sale, inheritance, partition) AnyROR Property card Ownership record for urban plots in City Survey areas AnyROR (urban section) Title deeds (sale deed chain) The legal transfers that make the seller the owner Seller’s originals; registration records Encumbrance search (EC) Registered transactions such as sales and mortgages affecting the property GARVI “Search with EC Report” NA order Permission to use agricultural land for non-agricultural purposes Seller; Revenue Department / iORA Approved plan and BU permission That the building was approved and is permitted to be used Municipal corporation, development authority or panchayat GujRERA registration That a new project is registered, plus its approvals and progress GujRERA portal Property tax and society dues No outstanding dues will pass to you Local body receipts; society NOC Seller identity and authority You are dealing with the real owner(s) or a valid power of attorney Originals of ID; registered PoA Land records: 7/12, 8A and mutation entries In Gujarat’s rural and peri-urban areas, the 7/12 extract (village form 7/12) is the basic record for a survey number. It shows the holder’s name, the area, and rights or charges recorded against the land. The 8A extract lists all the holdings of a khata (account) holder. Mutation entries (VF-6) record each change, such as a sale, an inheritance or a bank charge. You can view these free on AnyROR by district, taluka, village and survey number. Digitally signed copies and Revenue Department applications are handled on iORA. Warning signs: The seller’s name does not match the 7/12. A mutation entry is still pending or was disputed. A bank charge is recorded and has not been cleared. There are several co-owners, but only one is selling. Property card for city survey areas For urban land surveyed by a City Survey Office, ownership is recorded on a property card rather than a 7/12. AnyROR has an urban section for viewing property cards. Check the same things: the owner’s name, the area, and any recorded charges. Title deeds and the chain of ownership The land record shows who is recorded as holding the land. The title deeds show how they got it. An advocate normally traces the chain of registered sale deeds and other transfer documents for about 30 years and matches each step against the mutation entries. This title search is professional work. A clean online record does not replace it. Encumbrance search on GARVI The Inspector General of Registration’s GARVI portal offers a “Search with EC Report” service. It lists registered documents for a property by sub-registrar office, survey or city survey number, and year range. Limitation: it shows only registered documents. An unregistered agreement, a pending court case or an unpaid tax will not appear. That’s another reason to have an advocate do the title search. NA order: can the land be used for a home? Agricultural land in Gujarat needs non-agricultural (NA) permission before it can lawfully be used for housing or commercial building. For a plot or a building on former agricultural land, ask for the NA order and check that the permitted use matches yours. Applications and orders are handled through the Revenue Department, including online via iORA. Approved plan and BU permission For a built property, check that the building plan was approved by the local authority (municipal corporation, urban development authority or panchayat). Also check that Building Use (BU) permission was granted. BU permission is Gujarat’s equivalent of an occupancy certificate. Banks usually ask for the approved plan, the NA order and the BU permission before they lend. Warning sign: construction that differs from the approved plan, such as extra floors or a changed use, or a building that has been occupied without BU permission. GujRERA registration for new projects Under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, projects above the size threshold must be registered with the state RERA before they are advertised or sold. The threshold is land over 500 sq m or more than eight apartments. Agents who sell in registered projects must also register. On the GujRERA portal you can search registered projects and agents. A project’s page includes its approvals and quarterly progress updates. The RERA Act text is on India Code. Warning signs: No registration number in the advertising. The project name or promoter differs from the portal. Progress updates have stopped. Dues, society NOC and the seller’s identity Property tax: ask for the latest receipts from the local body, so unpaid tax doesn’t pass to you. Society or association: for flats, get a no-dues certificate and an NOC for the transfer, if the society requires one. Identity and authority: check every owner’s original ID. If someone is selling under a power of attorney, check that it is registered, still valid and covers the sale. Common mistakes Paying a token amount before seeing the 7/12 or property card and the title deeds. Treating an online record as final proof of ownership. Ignoring co-owners or legal heirs who are recorded but not signing. Buying on former agricultural land without seeing the NA order. Assuming a bank’s loan approval means the title is clean. Banks do their own checks, but those protect the bank. What to do next Collect copies of every document above from the seller before you negotiate seriously. View the 7/12, 8A, mutation entries or property card yourself on AnyROR, and compare them with what the seller gave you. Run the GARVI encumbrance search for the period your advocate advises. For new projects, check the GujRERA registration and the latest quarterly update. Have an advocate do a full title search before you sign an agreement or pay a significant amount. Also read: How to buy your first home in Gujarat. Sources AnyROR (Revenue Department, Government of Gujarat) — https://anyror.gujarat.gov.in/ — accessed 23 Oct 2026. iORA (Integrated Online Revenue Applications) — https://iora.gujarat.gov.in/ — accessed 23 Oct 2026. GARVI (Inspector General of Registration, Gujarat) — https://garvi.gujarat.gov.in/ — accessed 23 Oct 2026. Gujarat Real Estate Regulatory Authority — https://gujrera.gujarat.gov.in/ — accessed 23 Oct 2026. The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, sections 3, 9 and 10 — https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/2158/1/a2016-16.pdf
